questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The most crucial was the chance to study political science in Taiwan due to its geopolitical relations to China. I hoped to gain a better understanding of Taiwan during my exchange. Also I had to visit a place where I could receive Chinese lessons, so Taiwan was a good choice for this as well.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was super easy, we got plenty of mails beforehand preparing us for the introductionary days at NTU.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had been given a student volunteer contact which gave me a great introduction and explanation of how things worked in Taiwan as well as on the university itself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used an app/website called Zuyou. It's great for finding studio apartments in Taipei since it is available in both English and Chinese.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That it is kind of expensive if you want to live close to the university in an off-campus accomodation. The benefits are worth it, though, if you value privacy and being close to everything. The dorms are far away and usually consists of 4-people rooms.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was pretty impractical, as there weren't that many courses tought in English and it was not allowed to have overlapping classes. It made finding enough courses equal to 30 ECTS kind of difficult.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: At NTU there are two main rounds of course selections. The first round you pick as many courses as you can. Once you get the results of which of these courses you have been enrolled in, you can decide on which of these courses you actually want to settle with. This second election ends a few weeks into the semester, which gives you a chance to test out different courses before making your final decision.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Classmates, teacher PA's and the student volunteers could help out.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got pretty much all the classes I wanted, except for one, since it overlapped with another class.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My advice is to select as many courses as possible in the first round. If you have just the slightest interest in the course, apply for it. You can always remove course you don't need or want afterwards. Also be aware, since there are many hidden requirements for courses which means you can select them, but you will be declined afterwards, so if you don't select a lot, you will end up lacking enough courses to get enough credits.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think the academic level in terms of political science at bachelor-level courses were too low. Luckily it was possible to take graduate-level political science courses, which had a much higher level and were much more interesting.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The bachelor-level courses were dissapointing in terms of the academic level. The graduate-level courses, however, were very interesting and had great teachers.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The biggest difference is the amount of classes. I'm used to having 3-4 different courses per semester at UCPH, whereas at NTU I had 8, which means I had way more hours at the university sitting in class than at UCPH. Also, the grading system is very different, where at UCPH it's usually just the final exam that accounts for the total grade, at NTU it is a mix of attendance, mid-terms, homework, final exam, etc. that makes up the total grade. This gave less opportunity for me to decide on which classes I had to attend, since I had to attend every class in order to not lose scoring. I definitely prefer the UCPH style of course and grade structuring.
The teaching style varied greatly, with some professors having a very hands-on approach and not letting students have a lot of freedom, where other professors gave zero instructions at all and gave students pretty much full control of how to write assignments and do projects.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. General Chinese (Intermediate 1) 
2. Enhancing Chinese (Intermediate 1) 
3. Seminar on Political Economy of East Asia 
4. Seminar on Asian Democratization 
5. Public Administration
6. Seminar on China's Political and Economic Reform after Deng Xiaoping
7. Technological Developments, Politics and Society of China
8. Mini-Course: European Union and State Transformation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The course "Seminar on China's Political and Economic Reform after Deng Xiaoping" was amazing. The professor was great and the subjects we went through were very interesting. If you have interest in Chinese politics, this course will enhance your knowledge greatly. The same goes for "Technological Developments, Politics and Society of China", which also touched upon political developments in China, but with a focus on the effects that technology has had on China.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None really.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was super cheap, but since there was no kitchen in my studio apartment I had to buy everything on the streets, which ended up costing more than I expected initially.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: NTU has amazing sports opportunities, if you can think of a sport, they got a club for it you can join. There are plenty of gyms for working out and many bars where you can hang out with friends over a beer.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were courses offered which focused on exploring Taiwan, these courses were made to let students see Taiwan and engage in the culture. 
There were plenty of clubs for everything from football to archery to calligraphy. Everything had a club you could join. I personally tried rugby and handball.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Join a sports-club, it's a great way to meet the locals. In the handball club/team I was the only foreigner which gave me plenty of chances to practice Chinese and understand local culture. 
Taiwan is also great for hiking if you're into that.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel around Taiwan, explore Taipei, go to bars, travel abroad to Korea, Japan, Vietnam, etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, be respectful, don't be too loud, make an effort to understand the norms of Taiwan and you will find it is amazing.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take the initiative, they are quite introverted

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Mostly the language barrier, Taiwanese are generally not that great at English, so if you don't speak that much Chinese it can be challenging to communicate. The social culture is also different in my opinion, but it's about letting go of your own way of doing things and instead embrace the local customs if you want to make friends.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The respect for elderly and simply how nice everyone were. At the beginning it felt fake, but as you become accustomed it just feels natural and you start to replicate it.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Bring summer clothes, an umbrella and a wallet that handles bills and coins!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Regardless of your level of Chinese, it is worth to take the language courses. They are a great way to meet new people from class and also gives you tools to use when in Taiwan.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I've made from every part of the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The hardest was getting used to having so many classes, since it was so different from my experience at UCPH

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
